capture.final_message:
Treat the outer conjunction componentwise, and in each `Iff` show both propositions independently true.

For the first component, use the subgroup dichotomy for the real circle \(\mathbb R/p\mathbb Z\) with \(p>0\): every subgroup is either dense or finite cyclic. More precisely:

- If \(s\) is dense, it cannot equal \(\mathbb Z a\) for an element \(a\) of finite positive additive order.
- If \(s\) is not dense, its closure is a proper closed subgroup of the circle, hence finite cyclic. Since a dense subset of a finite space is the whole space, \(s\) itself equals this closure. Thus \(s=\mathbb Z a\) for some generator \(a\) with `addOrderOf a ≠ 0`, contradicting the stated condition.

The assumption \(p>0\) is essential here because it gives the usual nondegenerate circle and its classification of proper closed subgroups. The other side of this first `Iff`, surjectivity of `Quot.mk`, follows directly by quotient induction: every quotient element has a representative.

For the second component, recognize \(\pi_0(X)\) as a quotient of the set of \(0\)-simplices. Hence its canonical map `SSet.π₀.mk` is surjective by quotient induction. The opposite side is exactly the computation rule for `Quotient.liftOn'`: on the class represented by \(x\), the descended function evaluates to \(f(x)\).

Thus the proof can be organized around one substantive intermediate result—the dense-or-finite-cyclic classification of circle subgroups—while all quotient statements are canonical representative/computation properties.
